prime.problem: When a job is too slow, the easy fix is a faster machine or tighter code. Both divide the run time by a fixed number, so an n² algorithm on a 1000× faster computer still loses by 17.2× at n = 10⁷, and by more every time n grows.
prime.fits: Fourth estimation card. Back-of-envelope told you whether a design fits; this card says which lever to pull when it doesn't. Its model T = c·f(n)/s frames the next two cards: compilers shrink c, vectorization shrinks c a lot in Python, neither touches f(n).
prime.goal: Given two machine/algorithm pairs, compute who wins at a given n, find the crossover, and explain why the algorithm is the lever whose gain grows.

attend: Which of the three knobs (s, c, f(n)) changes the shape of the curve, and which only scale it?
Why does A ÷ B grow almost linearly in n, and what formula does the card give for it?
Below which n does the fast machine with insertion sort win, and by how much at n = 1,000?
How many years of hardware progress, and of compiler progress, does A's 1000× head start represent?
Once an algorithm is already optimal, where do the remaining wins come from?

must: Run time = c · f(n) / s → hardware changes s and tuning or compilers change c → both divide every run by a fixed factor → only the algorithm changes f(n), so only its gain grows with n
A ÷ B = 2n² · 10⁷ / (50 n lg n · 10¹⁰) = n / (25,000 lg n) → grows almost linearly → B wins 17.2× at 10⁷ and 1,338× at 10⁹ despite 1000× slower hardware and 25× more instructions per step
Constants still matter below the crossover → A wins for n < 471,146 (250× at n = 1,000) → which is why Timsort sorts short runs with insertion sort, then merges
Proebsting: hardware ~60%/yr vs compilers ~4%/yr → 1000× takes ~15 years of hardware or ~176 years of compilers → waiting for faster tools rarely rescues a bad algorithm
elevated: The source's n log n needs log₂ to give 1,163 s; natural log gives 806 s → a stated base changes an estimate by 1.44× → always say which log

compress.prompt: From memory, write T = c·f(n)/s, fill in A's and B's values, and compute T for both at n = 10⁷. Then say in two sentences why B wins and when it doesn't.
checklist: speed and c scale; f(n) sets growth
B wins by n / (25,000 lg n): 17.2× here
below n ≈ 471,146 the fast machine wins

retrieve.q: Explain why micro-tuning A's inner loop can never make it beat B at large n, even though A's constant is already 25× leaner.
answer: tuning only lowers c, a fixed factor
the ratio n / (25,000 lg n) keeps growing with n
for any fixed c there is an n beyond which B wins

retrieve.q: Walk through computing B's time for n = 10⁷, including the log.
Your data is always under 10,000 items. Should you still switch to the n log n algorithm on the slow machine? What does the card's table say?
answer: no: below the crossover A wins (20 ms vs 0.66 s at 10⁴)
the right choice depends on n
combine: small inputs with the low-constant algorithm, large with the low-growth one (Timsort's hybrid)

compare.q: The merge-sort card explains why it's n log n; this card uses that fact as a technology. What does merge sort pay for its growth advantage, and when does that price bite?
answer: log₂ n passes of one merge each: n log n
extra O(n) memory and a larger constant than insertion sort
it bites on small inputs (below the crossover) and when memory is tight

compare.q: The trade-offs card found break-even points in n (8.3 M addresses); this card finds one at 471,146 items. What makes both answers depend on n, and what would move each one?
answer: each option has a different fixed cost and a different growth
the break-even is where the two cost curves cross
bitmap/set moves with the universe size; this one moves with the speed gap and the constants

predict.q: Computer A gets another 10× faster (10¹¹ instructions/s), everything else the same. Before computing: does B still win at n = 10⁷, and roughly where does the crossover move, up 10×, or more?
predict.answer: B still wins at 10⁷, now 2,000 s vs 1,162.7 s (1.7×). The crossover moves from 471,146 to about 5,604,542, almost 12× higher, a bit more than 10× because n/lg n grows slightly slower than n. More hardware pushes the crossover out; it never removes it.

apply.task: Give B a better programmer: c = 5 instead of 50, same slow machine. (1) Compute B's time at n = 10⁷ and the new A ÷ B. (2) Reuse the card's crossover() binary search (with hi large enough) to find the new crossover. (3) Say in one sentence which knob you just changed and why the ratio moved by exactly that factor.
apply.done: B takes about 116.3 s, A ÷ B ≈ 172×, the crossover drops to 38,038, and your sentence says c is a constant factor, so the ratio moves by exactly 50 / 5 = 10× at every n.
